Another day, another commission

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A commission here, a commission there, but where are the prosecutors? Everywhere you look, there's a retired judge with no prosecutorial powers having a conversation with some of the foot soldiers

Unique Selling Point:
We have the testimonies on record of people who may not have agreed to interviews

Summary:
We take a look at some of the findings coming out of the state capture commission and ask what happens next? Where are the prosecutors?



Further information:
These are the views of deputy Editor of the Financial Mail Sikonathi Mantshantsha. Many agree, commissions of inquiry are coming out of our ears. In a single week - The Zondo commission on State Capture, The Nugent inquiry into SARS, the verdict on the social grants inquiry ordered by the Constitutional court- and the imminent publication of the report on parliaments public enterprises committee inquiry.

And those who did appear before parliament were the lowly foot soldiers who carried out the instructions of the masterminds as they brazenly looted Eskom into bankruptcy. And those masterminds, either showed parliament the middle finger, or were not summoned to appear.

After losing hundreds of billions of rand's to the biggest and most systemic organised crime operation in recent memory, SA has turned its attention to commissions. President Cyril Ramaphosa seems to have also fallen into the trap of governing through commissions.

Meanwhile, the masterminds live large in sunny locations enjoying their loot, and the most prominent suspects hold rallies and threaten their comrades with the fires of hell if they dare point out their corruption.

What are the police doing? Where are the state security agencies? All forms of crime seem to be spiralling out of control

Just like retired judge Robert Nugent's Sars inquiry, neither the parliamentary probe into Eskom nor Zondo's commission will directly convict anyone.What the commissions produce will only be recommendations. At most, the findings will recommend that the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) bring criminal charges. Thus no thief is losing any sleep.

Despite the mountains of evidence about the corruption that has bankrupted or threatens to bankrupt many municipalities and state-owned companies like Eskom, SAA, PetroSA, Denel, the SABC, the Passenger Rail Agency of SA, SA Express and Transnet, not a single arrest has been made. There's not a prosecutor in sight. No law enforcement agencies. Nothing.
Even the mock arrests in the R220m Estina dairy theft have been shown up for what they really are. It seems the Hawks' case has been deliberately undermined from within, to let the suspects off the hook.

The NPA and its chief Shaun Abrahams are sitting on their imaginary laurels while criminals are on the rampage.
Which leads one to ask: what is the SA Police Service doing? Where are the prosecutorial services? Where are the state security agencies? These sectors employ more than 300,000 people to enforce the law and prevent crime. Yet all forms of crime seem to be spiralling out of control.

Script:


Another day, Another commission. Final Script TX 9th September 2018

Commentary One
Day 8 of the state capture inquiry. Phumla Williams, acting director General of GCIS is ripping into her former minister, Faith Muthambi

Phumla Williams
Minister Muthambi wanted to be addressed as honourable

Commentary Two
She told the commission how she was bullied, demoted, how money was wasted, and supply chains manipulated, and how the minister insisted she should always be addressed as the honourable minister, even as it appeared the minister's actions seemed quite the opposite

Phumla Williams
I took the trouble to check the protocol, and I was assured that ministers cannot expect to be called honourable, outside parliament.

Commentary Three
Monday was day 9 of the inquiry, and Williams continued under oath
Pumla
I had to accept that I am dealing with an enemy that is coming to steal in our country

Commentary Four
Williams described how the stress of working under Muthambi for three years, reignited panic attacks that she first experienced after being tortured by apartheid security forces.

Phumla
I don't think that woman was interested in serving the people of South Africa, I don't think that woman was interested in preserving the resources of this country and that is why I said I will be failing the people of South Africa if I allow the thief to get away with it.

Commentary Five
Afterwards she told us, it wasn't an easy decision to testify

Phumla Williams
I am hoping Derek that it will not be in vain. It has taken me a helluva lot to summon the courage to come and tell my story

Derek Link
A lot of what has been heard at the commission has been heard before, but it's in the detail, the massive bribes, the threats the arrogance, that you get an idea of the grand masterplan that saw the Gupta's spread their tentacles into just about every aspect of the state



Commentary six
Themba Maseko, is former CEO of Government communications. Only 18 months after former President Zuma was sworn in, Maseko came up against the Gupta brothers

Themba Maseko
There was a parallel state in place, a parallel system of system of government

Commentary seven
GCIS did the media buying of all national government departments, with a large budget of R600 million. But the Gupta's were starting the New age and they wanted the entire R600 million. "This is how things are going to work," they told him.

Themba
And your only job is to make sure the money comes to me and the new age newspaper
Vincent Maleka SC
Seems to be someone is rewriting your official duties?
Themba
He was basically giving me an instruction which I found totally unacceptable and unlawful

Commentary eight
Maseko's refusals were followed by threats

Themba Maseko
he will speak to my seniors and make sure I am sorted out and make sure I am replaced with people who will co-operate

Commentary nine
Sure enough, within months, he was given the boot. Replaced by well- known Gupta ally, Mzwanele Manyi who was downstairs waiting for his parking bay almost immediately after Maseko was sent packing

Themba
I never even had the opportunity to pack my office, that is how urgent the move had to be!

Commentary ten
In 2016 former public protector Thuli Madonsela, was unable to complete her investigation on her State of Capture report and recommended a commission to complete the work.
Two years later that onerous task falls on the shoulders of deputy chief justice Zondo. But he can only make recommendations.

Link
But where are the prosecutors? Where are hawks? Well missing in action it seems

Commentary eleven
In a recent opinion piece Deputy Editor of the Financial Mail Sikonathi Mantshantsha writes: "Enough of the commissions where are the prosecutors?"

Sikonathi
We will get nothing from the Zondo commission of Inquiry, as we got nothing from the parliamentary inquiry into state capture, Eskom, Transnet, we got nothing from the SABC, we got nothing from arms deal inquiry, we got nothing from Marikana, the judges will make their findings and tell us what happened, which is what we already know- so what!

Commentary twelve
Not everyone agrees. Civil Society organisation OUTA is currently preparing its documents to submit to the commission

Wayne
We don't blame people for feeling that way, but we believe that these commissions are necessary and will have a positive impact on this country

Commentary thirteen
Last year OUTA laid charges against several people implicated in state capture. Faith Muthambi was charged with treason for sharing confidential cabinet information with the Gupta's. But OUTA have been frustrated with the Hawks progress. The hawks did not respond to our questions

Wayne
These are formal charges provided to the Hawks and these are files like this- not a two pager.

Sikonathi Mantshantsha
The outcome that many right- thinking and patriotic South Africans want, is someone jailed for state capture, as much of the money that was stolen recovered

Commentary fourteen
But nothing has happened. Take the case of Vytjie Mentor.

Vytjie
I asked him how he could make me a minister, he said they often put word to the president for people to become ministers

Commentary Fourteen A
She has told her story many times of how former President Zuma was at the Gupta home when they offered her a cabinet position, in return for cancelling the SAA route to India so they could profit. We spoke to Senior counsel Nazeer Cassim

Derek
Do you see any of the evidence leading to criminal prosecutions?
Nazzir
I am concerned. Mrs. Mentor makes a full affidavit two years ago to a policeman -its sufficient to found a basis to charge the culprits. What happens now is two years later she must give a narrative on her affidavit in a very expensive forum and giving for want of a better term, the bad guys an opportunity to now hear her version. I don't see what purpose that is serving.

Commentary fifteen
The NPA told Carte Blanche they will wait for the commission to make its findings but that could take another two years! Meanwhile Nazeer Cassim has tallied up the costs.

Nazzir
I would estimate that it is probably running in the region of perhaps R200 000 per day and that is conservative estimate. Its projected to be close to R300 million for the first year and if it runs to the second year its R600 million. To me that is a lot of money and you know we are a poor nation. Do we need this luxury?

Derek
Could the Hawks start arresting people now instead of waiting for the commission to grind to a halt
Nazzir
Of course, in my view there is sufficient material already to charge people

Commentary sixteen
But the Hawks and the NPA were compromised by the Gupta's, as former Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas told the commission under oath.

Mcebisi Jonas
He said, and I quote we are in control of everything. The NPA, the HAWKS, the NIA and the old man will do anything we tell him to do. He said that the old man intended to appoint me as the minister of finance

Commentary Seventeen
So the irony was not lost on South Africans this week, when Ajay Gupta through his lawyer Mike Hellens called the Hawks an incompetent national embarrassment. Many would agree. Why can't we build strong institutions asks Mantshantsha?

Sikonathi
Strong institutions are what make for strong democracies - strong democracies are what makes prosperous nations.

Commentary Eighteen
At the Hawks, new head Godfrey Lebeya is trying, slowly. Last week they told parliament they will fast track state capture investigations. People like Jonas, showed them where to start a long time ago.

Mcebisi Jonas
He also said that if I worked with them I would become very rich, and he could immediately offer me R600 million.




Commentary nineteen
By the end of this week, those already implicated fought back. Ajay Gupta, through his lawyer Mike Hellens, said he would only testify via video link, presumably from Dubai.

And Next week we will know if deputy chief justice Zondo will allow the Gupta's and Duduzane Zuma to cross examine the state capture witnesses.

Sikonathi
Judge Zondo has been saying people must come forward. At some point he should invite them and if they refuse then subpoena them otherwise there is no point in the commission. He should be talking to the people who don't want to talk to him

Commentary Twenty
Former president Zuma has not even applied to cross examine the witnesses who have placed him squarely at the scene of the crime of state capture

Sikonathi
he should be dragged kicking and screaming to answer questions before the commission

Commentary Twenty- One
Faith Muthambi hasn't applied either to cross examine, her accuser Pumla Williams, but she has released a statement that Williams is one of the most shameful manipulators and liars that she has ever had the displeasure to encounter

Derek
Now you want Faith Muthambi to come here and give her testimony?

Pumla
You know this would be the happiest moment for me because I am still left with questions that have not been answered!

THE END 10: 07

PROMO ONE 10 seconds
Two years ago the former public protector recommended a commission to complete her work into state capture. But will the testimonies lead to prosecutions

PROMO TWO 15 seconds
Finally the Hawks announce they will fast track state capture investigations
Derek
Could the Hawks start arresting people now instead of waiting for the commission to grind to a halt
Nazeer
Of course, in my view there is sufficient material already to charge people

PROMO THREE 15 seconds
Two weeks into the Zondo commission and damning testimonies have been heard under oath.

She wanted to be called honourable

Phumla Williams
It has taken me a helluva lot to summon the courage to come and tell my story

PROMO FOUR 30 seconds

Sikonathi
We will get nothing from the Zondo commission of Inquiry, as we got nothing from the parliamentary inquiry into state capture, Eskom, Transnet, we got nothing from the SABC, we got nothing from arms deal inquiry, we got nothing from Marikana, the judges will make their findings and tell us what happened, which is what we already know

Wayne
We don't blame people for feeling that way, but we believe that these commissions are necessary and will have a positive impact on this country

metadata.Further information: These are the views of deputy Editor of the Financial Mail Sikonathi Mantshantsha. Many agree, commissions of inquiry are coming out of our ears. In a single week - The Zondo commission on State Capture, The Nugent inquiry into SARS, the verdict on the social grants inquiry ordered by the Constitutional court- and the imminent publication of the report on parliaments public enterprises committee inquiry. And those who did appear before parliament were the lowly foot soldiers who carried out the instructions of the masterminds as they brazenly looted Eskom into bankruptcy. And those masterminds, either showed parliament the middle finger, or were not summoned to appear. After losing hundreds of billions of rand's to the biggest and most systemic organised crime operation in recent memory, SA has turned its attention to commissions. President Cyril Ramaphosa seems to have also fallen into the trap of governing through commissions. Meanwhile, the masterminds live large in sunny locations enjoying their loot, and the most prominent suspects hold rallies and threaten their comrades with the fires of hell if they dare point out their corruption. What are the police doing? Where are the state security agencies? All forms of crime seem to be spiralling out of control Just like retired judge Robert Nugent's Sars inquiry, neither the parliamentary probe into Eskom nor Zondo's commission will directly convict anyone.What the commissions produce will only be recommendations. At most, the findings will recommend that the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) bring criminal charges. Thus no thief is losing any sleep. Despite the mountains of evidence about the corruption that has bankrupted or threatens to bankrupt many municipalities and state-owned companies like Eskom, SAA, PetroSA, Denel, the SABC, the Passenger Rail Agency of SA, SA Express and Transnet, not a single arrest has been made. There's not a prosecutor in sight. No law enforcement agencies. Nothing. Even the mock arrests in the R220m Estina dairy theft have been shown up for what they really are. It seems the Hawks' case has been deliberately undermined from within, to let the suspects off the hook. The NPA and its chief Shaun Abrahams are sitting on their imaginary laurels while criminals are on the rampage. Which leads one to ask: what is the SA Police Service doing? Where are the prosecutorial services? Where are the state security agencies? These sectors employ more than 300,000 people to enforce the law and prevent crime. Yet all forms of crime seem to be spiralling out of control.
